title: Degree-conditioned anneal offsets reshape certified-optimum sampling for minimum vertex cover
abstract: Quantum annealers can sample degenerate optima unevenly, so the composition of finite-read output matters when multiple solutions are sought. We investigate whether problem structure can steer this output through node-dependent anneal offsets for Minimum Vertex Cover (MVC). In MVC, vertex degree equals the number of incident edge-cover constraints and therefore measures local constraint participation. We use this relation to define degree-conditioned offset-scheduled quantum annealing (DC-OSQA), a static rule assigning more negative offsets to vertices with larger max-normalized degree. Experiments used a D-Wave Advantage2 system1 quantum processing unit (QPU). For each graph, DC-OSQA was compared with a zero-offset baseline using the same MVC encoding, fixed physical embedding, majority-vote chain decoding, and 1000-read budget. A sampled bitstring was counted as a certified candidate only if it represented a feasible vertex cover and its cardinality matched the minimum independently certified by integer linear programming. Across 120 paired comparisons on sparse Barabasi-Albert graphs with two attachments per added vertex and graph sizes N = 70-150, DC-OSQA increased the mean number of distinct certified candidates from 171.7 to 455.8 and the mean number of complete-linkage Hamming-distance families from 22.5 to 80.0; paired gains were positive at every tested size. These shifts, together with lower empirical concentration, indicate a change in the composition of the observed certified support. At N = 150, the degree-aligned assignment exceeded the within-instance mean over 20 random reassignments of the same offset values in 19 of 20 graphs for certified-support size and all 20 graphs for Hamming families. Within the tested ensemble, these results show that an MVC-specific degree rule changes the certified optima observed within a fixed QPU read budget.
summary: This paper demonstrates that tailoring the quantum annealing schedule using vertex degrees—a structural property of the Minimum Vertex Cover problem—can significantly increase the diversity and count of certified optimal solutions found on a quantum annealer. By implementing degree-conditioned offsets, the authors show they can steer the sampling process to explore a richer set of degenerate optima within a fixed computational budget.
main_problem: The study investigates how incorporating problem-specific structural information, derived from vertex degrees, can steer the composition of certified optimal solutions sampled by quantum annealers for the Minimum Vertex Cover (MVC) problem.
main_result: Degree-conditioned annealing offsets (DC-OSQA) significantly increased the mean number of distinct certified candidates and Hamming-distance families compared to a zero-offset baseline on sparse Barabási–Albert graphs.
method: The authors implemented DC-OSQA by assigning anneal offsets proportional to the vertex degree, comparing its performance against a standard zero-offset quantum annealing baseline.
model_or_system: The work uses quantum annealers, specifically the D-Wave Advantage2 QPU, to solve the MVC problem encoded as a QUBO. The core technique involves modifying the annealing Hamiltonian via degree-dependent offsets.
key_observables: Mean number of distinct certified candidates, mean number of complete-linkage Hamming-distance families, and the difference in effective support ($\Delta S_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Graph size N (70-150), offset scale $\alpha$, and the fixed QPU read budget.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to sparse Barabási–Albert graphs and assumes a fixed, finite QPU read budget.
figures_summary: Figures summarize the gains of DC-OSQA over baselines in unique certified candidates and Hamming families, showing positive gains across tested sizes.
paper_structure: The paper develops the DC-OSQA protocol based on vertex degrees, compares its performance against a zero-offset baseline using quantitative metrics (certified support size), and concludes that the degree rule successfully alters the observed set of optimal solutions.
why_interesting: The explicit manipulation of the quantum annealing schedule using problem structure (degree) to control the sampling distribution of degenerate ground states is highly relevant to understanding the limitations and potential enhancements of quantum optimization algorithms.
